title: Luke 8:1–21
context: Women who have received healing help support Jesus’ traveling ministry as he proclaims the kingdom. The sower, the lamp, and the description of Jesus’ true family connect fruitful hearing with perseverance and obedience, while raising difficult questions about given understanding and temporary belief.

verses.text: Soon afterwards, he went about through cities and villages, preaching and bringing the good news of God’s Kingdom. With him were the twelve,
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus brings the kingdom’s good news through cities and villages with the twelve. Arminian readers see proclamation inviting many communities to hear and respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize the announced kingdom. The word soon pictured as seed is already being carried among actual hearers through Jesus’ traveling ministry.

verses.text: and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out;
verses.arminianNotes: Healed and delivered women accompany Jesus, including Mary Magdalene. Arminian readers see recipients of mercy participating in ministry rather than disappearing once their need is met.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize these women as valued participants. Neither this verse nor the preceding meal identifies Mary as the unnamed sinful woman of chapter 7.

verses.text: and Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others who served them from their possessions.
verses.arminianNotes: Joanna, Susanna, and others support the group from their possessions. Arminian readers see practical generosity as meaningful participation, not a lesser response to grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise honor material service. The WEB prints them, with a footnote reporting him in the Textus Receptus; its wording is retained without diminishing service to Jesus.

verses.text: When a great multitude came together and people from every city were coming to him, he spoke by a parable:
verses.arminianNotes: A growing crowd hears a parable. Arminian readers note that exposure to Jesus’ teaching does not make every response identical; attentive reception matters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish gathering around Jesus from fruitful hearing. The soils explain differing responses to the same word rather than different messages for different groups.

verses.text: “The farmer went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the road, and it was trampled under foot, and the birds of the sky devoured it.
verses.arminianNotes: Seed on the road is trampled and eaten before bearing fruit. Arminian readers see the danger of hearing without retaining the word, as Jesus will explain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the seed’s vulnerability while exposed. The image should follow Jesus’ explanation rather than speculative significance assigned to every incidental detail.

verses.text: Some seed fell on the rock, and as soon as it grew, it withered away, because it had no moisture.
verses.arminianNotes: Seed on rock grows but withers for lack of moisture. Arminian readers see that a beginning alone does not establish the enduring fruitfulness Jesus seeks.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish visible growth from lasting rootedness. Verse 13 makes the temporary character of this reception central to the warning.

verses.text: Some fell amid the thorns, and the thorns grew with it and choked it.
verses.arminianNotes: Thorns grow alongside the seed and choke it. Arminian readers see competing attachments suppressing what has been heard without an immediate, open rejection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the word must bear fruit, not merely coexist with other priorities. Jesus names ordinary cares and pleasures as well as riches.

verses.text: Some fell into the good ground and grew and produced one hundred times as much fruit.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!”
verses.arminianNotes: Good soil yields abundantly, and Jesus summons attentive hearing. Arminian readers see hope joined to responsibility, not a promise that casual listening is enough.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize the word’s abundant fruit. The summons addresses the crowd seriously, while the following explanation credits understanding as a gift.

verses.text: Then his disciples asked him, “What does this parable mean?”
verses.arminianNotes: The disciples ask for understanding rather than assume the story explains itself. Arminian readers see responsive hearing that seeks further instruction from Jesus.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize dependence on the teacher who gives understanding. Disciples still need to ask, listen, and receive his explanation.

verses.text: He said, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of God’s Kingdom, but to the rest it is given in parables, that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
verses.arminianNotes: Understanding is given, while Isaiah 6:9 associates parables with nonperception. Arminian readers often understand judicial hardening of resistant hearers, not denial that grace genuinely calls them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize God’s sovereign distinction in giving understanding and withholding it in judgment. Both affirm judgment and responsibility; this is more than a neutral teaching technique.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm that understanding is given and that the Isaiah quotation speaks of judgment, not merely an illustrative method. Arminian readers commonly stress judicial hardening in response to resistance; Reformed readers stress sovereign discrimination in granting understanding. Neither reading eliminates human responsibility.

verses.text: “Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus identifies the seed as God’s word. Arminian readers see a gracious message that must be heard and held rather than replaced by speculation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize the word as God’s appointed means of fruitfulness. The issue lies in its reception, not a deficiency in the seed itself.

verses.text: Those along the road are those who hear; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their heart, that they may not believe and be saved.
verses.arminianNotes: The devil removes the word so hearers do not believe and receive salvation. Arminian readers see opposition to a genuinely saving message and urgency about attentive hearing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the connection between belief and salvation and the reality of satanic opposition. External hearing is not identical to enduring reception.

verses.text: Those on the rock are they who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but these have no root. They believe for a while, then fall away in time of temptation.
verses.arminianNotes: These hearers receive joyfully, believe temporarily, and fall away under temptation. Many classical Arminian readers see a real believing response that can be abandoned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers distinguish temporary faith from saving, rooted faith, pointing to the absence of roots. Both warn that initial joy is no substitute for enduring trust under trial.
verses.keyContrast: Both distinguish enduring faith from a joyful beginning that collapses under trial. Many classical Arminian readers see genuine faith later abandoned; Reformed readers see temporary belief without the root of regeneration. The dispute concerns the initial belief’s character, not the seriousness of falling away.

verses.text: What fell among the thorns, these are those who have heard, and as they go on their way they are choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life; and they bring no fruit to maturity.
verses.arminianNotes: Cares, riches, and pleasures choke growth before fruit matures. Arminian readers warn against gradual spiritual suffocation as well as sudden rejection under temptation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise warn that ordinary preoccupations can expose barren reception. Wealth and pleasure are not reliable signs of spiritual health, and anxiety can also consume attention.

verses.text: Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.
verses.arminianNotes: Fruitful hearers retain the word and persevere. Arminian readers understand a grace-enabled, continuing response, not hearts made good independently of God’s help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers understand the good heart and enduring fruit as effects of renewing and preserving grace. Both insist on steadfast reception, not merely momentary emotion.

verses.text: “No one, when he has lit a lamp, covers it with a container or puts it under a bed; but puts it on a stand, that those who enter in may see the light.
verses.arminianNotes: A lamp is lit to give light, not conceal it. Arminian readers connect the image with receiving Jesus’ teaching in ways that illuminate life and serve others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise understand revelation as meant to bear visible effect. The image balances concealment without erasing the warning about unresponsive hearing.

verses.text: For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, nor anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
verses.arminianNotes: What is hidden will be disclosed. Arminian readers hear that present concealment is not final and that appearances cannot provide lasting security.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress ultimate disclosure. Within this teaching about hearing, the saying calls for integrity rather than confidence that concealed responses will remain unexposed.

verses.text: Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus warns hearers to attend carefully, since apparent possession can prove empty. Arminian readers see responsibility to continue receiving rather than presume upon earlier exposure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a serious warning against merely seeming to possess understanding. Such admonitions sustain attentive discipleship rather than excuse passive assurance.

verses.text: His mother and brothers came to him, and they could not come near him for the crowd.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus’ relatives cannot reach him through the crowd. Arminian readers see the setting for family defined around hearing God, not a command to despise natural kinship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish the obstacle from an accusation against the family. Luke does not explain their motives or invite speculation about hostility here.

verses.text: Some people told him, “Your mother and your brothers stand outside, desiring to see you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus is told that his mother and brothers seek him. Arminian readers see natural ties acknowledged before Jesus broadens the description of belonging.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note a teaching occasion. Access to Christ’s household does not depend on ancestry or the ability to get past a crowd.

verses.text: But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are these who hear the word of God and do it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus identifies family through hearing and doing God’s word. Arminian readers see obedient response as integral to belonging while denying that works purchase admission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see obedience as fruit and evidence of kinship through grace. Both affirm a family wider than blood relations without permitting neglect of relatives.
